CALIFORNIA CORPORATE STATUTORY MERGER — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc. and Beta Corp. · Acme, Inc.

RECITALS — STATUTORY MERGER OF CONSTITUENT CORPORATIONS
Acme, Inc. and Beta Corp. (each a constituent corporation) intend to merge into a single corporation under California's General Corporation Law, Chapter 11 (Merger), Cal. Corp. Code §§ 1100-1113. Upon the merger becoming effective, Acme, Inc. will be the surviving corporation, and the separate existence of each other constituent corporation will cease. This document records the agreement of merger between the constituent corporations and the corporate approvals obtained for it. It addresses the statutory merger procedure itself — a separate matter from whatever merger-approval, first-refusal, or transfer-restriction provisions may already appear in a constituent corporation's own bylaws, shareholder agreements, or buy-sell agreement, which govern only how that corporation's own internal decision to merge is made, not the statutory mechanics of the merger itself.

REQUIRED CONTENTS OF THE AGREEMENT OF MERGER
California law requires a merger of two or more corporations to proceed by a written agreement of merger, and it specifies what that agreement must contain. The agreement must state the terms and conditions of the merger; the name and place of incorporation of each constituent corporation and which of them is the surviving corporation; and the manner of converting the shares of each constituent corporation into shares or other securities of the surviving corporation — or, where shares are not converted solely into shares or securities of the surviving corporation, the cash, rights, securities, or other property the shareholders are instead to receive, whether in addition to or in lieu of surviving-corporation shares, or a statement that the shares are simply canceled without consideration. The statute also authorizes the agreement to include other terms and provisions the parties want, subject to a separate statutory equal-treatment rule for shares of the same class.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "The agreement shall state all of the following: (1) The terms and conditions of the merger."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1101(a), General Corporation Law, introductory requirement that the agreement of merger state all of the required terms (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1101.)
  "(3) The name and place of incorporation of each constituent corporation and which of the constituent corporations is the surviving corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1101(a)(3), General Corporation Law, agreement of merger must identify each constituent corporation and the surviving corporation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1101.)
  "(4) The manner of converting the shares of each of the constituent corporations into shares or other securities of the surviving corporation and, if any shares of any of the constituent corporations are not to be converted solely into shares or other securities of the surviving corporation, the cash, rights, securities, or other property which the holders of those shares are to receive in exchange for the shares, which cash, rights, securities, or other property may be in addition to or in lieu of shares or other securities of the surviving corporation, or that the shares are canceled without consideration."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1101(a)(4), General Corporation Law, agreement of merger must state the manner of converting shares (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1101.)

It does not address the separate short-form procedure for a parent corporation merging with a subsidiary it wholly or 90-percent owns, mergers where a foreign corporation or an "other business entity" (e.g., an LLC) is a constituent party, or mergers involving a social purpose corporation — each of which Chapter 11 itself carves out to separate provisions not independently verified here. This document also does not restate the equal-treatment rule for shares of the same class and series, which the statute states separately in the remainder of the same subdivision. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific corporation's merger, and not a claim about what terms any specific merger agreement should or must contain beyond this minimum required content. This document is informational only; it does not itself merge any corporations and does not draft or approve a specific agreement of merger.

BOARD AND SHAREHOLDER APPROVAL OF THE MERGER
A merger requires two layers of approval from each constituent corporation. First, the board of each corporation that desires to merge must approve the agreement of merger. Second, unless a narrower statutory exception applies, the principal terms of the merger must separately be approved by "the outstanding shares" of each class of each corporation whose board approval is required. Under California's own statutory definition of that phrase, approval by the outstanding shares means the affirmative vote of a majority of the outstanding shares entitled to vote, and it also includes the affirmative vote of a majority of the outstanding shares of each class or series separately entitled to vote as a class on the matter, plus any greater proportion — up to and including all shares of a class — that the corporation's own articles of incorporation require.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "The board of each corporation that desires to merge shall approve an agreement of merger."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1101(a), General Corporation Law, board approval of the agreement of merger (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1101.)
  "The principal terms of a reorganization shall be approved by the outstanding shares (Section 152) of each class of each corporation the approval of whose board is required under Section 1200"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1201(a), General Corporation Law, shareholder approval of the principal terms of a merger reorganization (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1201.)
  "Such approval shall include the affirmative vote of a majority of the outstanding shares of each class or series entitled, by any provision of the articles or of this division, to vote as a class or series on the subject matter being voted upon and shall also include the affirmative vote of such greater proportion (including all) of the outstanding shares of any class or series if such greater proportion is required by the articles or this division."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 152, General Corporation Law, statutory definition of "approved by the outstanding shares" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=152.)

In particular, this document does not address: the narrower board-only approval available for certain parent-subsidiary short-form mergers under a separate provision of this chapter; the exception (Cal. Corp. Code § 1201(b)) that removes the outstanding-shares-approval requirement for a corporation whose own shareholders will hold more than five-sixths of the resulting voting power; the heightened two-thirds vote that applies to a close corporation's shareholders in some circumstances; or the rule that all shareholders of a class must approve, unless given dissenters' rights, if the merger would make them personally liable for a constituent corporation's obligations. That dissenters'-rights safeguard is itself the subject of a separate document in this collection (California's statutory dissenters'/appraisal rights procedure), which this document does not restate. The three citations below are to three different, independently numbered statutory provisions — Cal. Corp. Code § 1101(a) (board approval), § 1201(a) (the outstanding-shares approval requirement for a merger reorganization), and § 152 (the statutory definition of "approved by the outstanding shares") — so they are independent sources, not subsections of a single section. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific corporation's merger, and not a claim about what approval any specific merger actually requires, which depends on the specific corporations, their articles of incorporation, and which of the statutory exceptions, if any, apply. This document is informational only and does not itself approve any merger.

EFFECT OF MERGER: SUCCESSION TO RIGHTS, PROPERTY, AND LIABILITIES
Once a merger under this chapter is effective, the statute specifies exactly what happens to each constituent corporation. The separate existence of each disappearing corporation ceases, and the surviving corporation succeeds — without any separate transfer being needed — to all of the rights and property of each disappearing corporation. At the same time, the surviving corporation becomes subject to all of the debts and liabilities of each disappearing corporation, in the same manner as if the surviving corporation had itself incurred those debts and liabilities. In other words, a merger does not let the surviving corporation pick up a disappearing corporation's assets while leaving its liabilities behind.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "Upon merger pursuant to this chapter the separate existence of the disappearing corporations ceases and the surviving corporation shall succeed, without other transfer, to all the rights and property of each of the disappearing corporations and shall be subject to all the debts and liabilities of each in the same manner as if the surviving corporation had itself incurred them."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1107(a), General Corporation Law, effect of merger: cessation of the disappearing corporation and succession to rights, property, and liabilities (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1107.)
  Known gap: This states the core successor-liability rule of Cal. Corp. Code § 1107(a) precisely as written; it does not overclaim beyond it. This document does not address the related provisions elsewhere in the same section — preservation of creditors' rights and liens on a disappearing corporation's property, continuation of pending litigation against the surviving corporation, or the separate local-agency-license-transfer and tax-return-assumption rules found in the rest of section 1107 and in section 1107.5 — which were not independently quoted here. This is a single statutory section (Cal. Corp. Code § 1107(a)); no additional independent source was sought for this specific rule. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific merger, and not a claim about the actual debts, liabilities, or property of any specific corporation. This document is informational only and does not itself effect any merger or transfer any right, property, debt, or liability.

FILING THE AGREEMENT OF MERGER AND ITS EFFECTIVE DATE
After the board and any required shareholder approval, the surviving corporation must file a copy of the agreement of merger with the California Secretary of State, along with an officers' certificate from each constituent corporation. That officers' certificate must state the total number of outstanding shares of each class entitled to vote on the merger and either that the required shareholder vote was obtained for the class or classes entitled to vote, or that the merger was instead entitled to be, and was, approved by the board alone under the statute's narrower board-only exception. The merger, and any amendment to the surviving corporation's articles set out in the agreement, becomes effective upon that filing — except that any instrument filed with the Secretary of State with respect to a corporation, including an agreement of merger, may instead specify a delayed effective date of up to 90 days after its filing date, and if no timely revocation certificate is filed to stop it, the instrument becomes effective on that later, specified date rather than on the filing date itself.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "After approval of a merger by the board and any approval of the outstanding shares (Section 152) required by Chapter 12 (commencing with Section 1200), the surviving corporation shall file a copy of the agreement of merger with an officers' certificate of each constituent corporation attached stating the total number of outstanding shares of each class entitled to vote on the merger, that the principal terms of the agreement in the form attached were approved by that corporation by a vote of a number of shares of each class which equaled or exceeded the vote required, specifying each class entitled to vote and the percentage vote required of each class, or that the merger agreement was entitled to be and was approved by the board alone under the provisions of Section 1201."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1103, General Corporation Law, filing the agreement of merger with an officers' certificate from each constituent corporation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1103.)
  "The merger and any amendment of the articles of the surviving corporation contained in the merger agreement shall thereupon be effective (subject to subdivision (c) of Section 110 and subject to the provisions of Section 1108) and the several parties thereto shall be one corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1103, General Corporation Law, the merger becomes effective upon that filing, subject to Section 110(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1103.)
  "Any instrument filed with respect to a corporation, other than original articles or instruments filed pursuant to Section 119, may provide that it is to become effective not more than 90 days subsequent to its filing date."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 110(c), General Corporation Law, an instrument filed with the Secretary of State (including a merger agreement) may specify a delayed effective date of up to 90 days (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=110.)

The citation to Cal. Corp. Code § 110(c) is to a separate, independently numbered section (California's general instrument-filing statute, not specific to mergers) and is an independent source. This document does not address the separate filing mechanics that apply when a foreign corporation is a constituent party (Cal. Corp. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific merger's filing, and not a substitute for the Secretary of State's own current official forms, fees, and filing instructions. This document is informational only and does not itself file anything with the California Secretary of State.

OFFICERS' CERTIFICATION AND SIGNATURES
The undersigned officer(s) of each constituent corporation certify, for filing with the agreement of merger, that: the total number of outstanding shares of each class of Acme, Inc. and Beta Corp. entitled to vote on the merger, and the vote obtained, were as follows: 1,000,000 shares outstanding; 750,000 shares voted in favor; and that this vote equaled or exceeded the vote required for approval, or that the merger was instead entitled to be, and was, approved by the board alone under California's applicable statutory exception.

On behalf of the board of each constituent corporation, the undersigned further certify that the board approved the agreement of merger on September 5, 2026, and, if shareholder approval was separately required, that the outstanding shares approved the agreement's principal terms on September 12, 2026.

Jordan Lee, Chief Executive Officer
